screens.title: Backup and Restore Strategies
screens.subtitle: Designing reliable, testable backups across AWS services for durable recovery

narration.text: In this chapter we'll focus on the practical patterns that make backups dependable and recoverable. Backups are the simplest and most cost-effective layer of disaster recovery, but they are only useful when you can restore reliably. You will learn how EBS snapshots and AMIs let you capture EC2 state, how RDS automated backups and transaction logs enable point‑in‑time recovery, and how S3 features like versioning and cross‑region replication protect object data. We also cover centralized control using AWS Backup and automation with Data Lifecycle Manager for scheduled EBS snapshots and cross‑region copies. I will explain why cross‑account copies are an important isolation mechanism, and why testing restores and enforcing encryption and IAM controls are non‑negotiable. Expect concrete examples: a DLM policy to snapshot production volumes and a practical backup plan JSON for cross‑region RDS copies. By the end of this lesson, you will be able to select the right AWS service for a given data type, automate retention rules, and create a testable restore process so backups become recoverable assets rather than forgotten buckets of data. Consider: when was the last time your organization restored a backup successfully? That experience informs every choice you'll make here.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Backups must be regular, encrypted, tested, and stored across regions and accounts when durability and isolation are required.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives map to tasks you'll do as an architect. First, you'll implement backup and restore procedures across AWS services, matching tools to data types and writing automated policies so snapshots and archives run without manual steps. Second, you'll configure cross‑region and cross‑account replication so critical backups survive regional failures and account compromise, and you'll learn the role of separate DR accounts. Third, you'll design automated schedules and lifecycle rules using AWS Backup and Data Lifecycle Manager, balancing retention for compliance against storage cost. Fourth, you'll establish regular restore testing and identify common pitfalls like untested backups, insufficient retention, or missing encryption. Each objective includes a short competency milestone so you can verify success: executing a DLM policy, creating a cross‑region backup copy, applying lifecycle transitions, and performing a restore drill. These objectives emphasize both automation and verification — backups alone do not protect you unless restores are validated and access controls are enforced. By mastering these objectives you will move from ad hoc snapshots to a repeatable, auditable backup program that reduces downtime and data loss risk.

keyIdea.title: Objective summary
keyIdea.text: Automate backups, replicate across region/account, enforce lifecycle and encryption, and test restores regularly.

screens.title: How these objectives help you
screens.subtitle: Mapping specific skills to on-the-job tasks and audits

narration.text: Knowing what to back up and how to back it up changes how you design systems. For example, by implementing automated EBS snapshots tied to resource tags, you can avoid manual snapshot errors and ensure that only production volumes are covered. Cross‑region and cross‑account strategies protect against correlated failures and accidental deletion: a vault in a separate account means a rogue user in your primary account cannot delete DR copies. Designing lifecycle rules reduces long‑term costs by moving older recovery points to Glacier or deep archive while retaining recent snapshots for quick restores. Finally, by routinely executing restore drills you will uncover common issues: missing IAM permissions, incorrect KMS key usage across accounts, or corrupted snapshots. Each objective maps to measurable tasks—write the DLM policy, create the AWS Backup plan with copy actions, configure S3 CRR with versioning enabled, and run a restore workflow from a snapshot to a new instance. These checks also support compliance audits and post‑incident reviews. The goal is repeatability: a documented, automated process that produces recoverable recovery points whenever you need them.

keyIdea.title: Why these skills matter
keyIdea.text: Automation, isolation, lifecycle management, and testing turn backups into reliable recovery mechanisms rather than paper policies.

Common pitfall

Pro tip
Use tags to target production resources and document retention rationale to avoid cost surprises.

screens.title: EBS Snapshots and AMIs
screens.subtitle: How volume snapshots and images form EC2 recovery points

narration.text: EBS snapshots are point‑in‑time copies of an EBS volume that are stored incrementally, meaning only changed blocks are saved after the first snapshot. This reduces storage and cost for frequent snapshots. When you need to restore, you create a new EBS volume from a snapshot and attach it to an instance. Amazon Machine Images, or AMIs, combine a snapshot of the root volume with launch configuration and mappings for other volumes, so you can quickly recreate a complete EC2 instance with software preinstalled. A practical distinction: snapshots are focused on block storage data and are ideal for restoring a volume or creating a volume baseline; AMIs are templates for launching instances at scale. A common misconception is thinking snapshots are automatically bootable images — a snapshot must be used to create a volume and an AMI packages the information needed to launch. Example: take daily EBS snapshots of a database volume, and also create periodic AMIs of application servers so you can redeploy identical server images after an outage. Key operational tips include encrypting snapshots, automating creation with DLM or AWS Backup, and tagging snapshots for retention and cost allocation. Takeaway: use snapshots for volume recovery and AMIs for rapid instance rebuilds; automate both and test restores to ensure they perform as expected.

keyIdea.title: EBS vs AMI
keyIdea.text: Use EBS snapshots for block-level recovery and AMIs to capture full instance launch configuration for quick rebuilds.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › EBS Snapshots and AMIs
Core Concept

EBS snapshots are incremental block backups

Snapshots capture changed blocks so repeated snapshots are storage-efficient. Use automation for consistent schedules.

Operation
Create snapshot → store incrementally in S3-backed storage → restore by creating a new EBS volume from snapshot.
AMI use case
Create AMIs for preconfigured servers so you can launch identical instances quickly after failure.
Key takeaway

Snapshots are storage-efficient backups; AMIs are full instance templates for fast redeployment.

Concrete example
Daily snapshot schedule for a production database volume, weekly AMI for app servers.
Restore walkthrough
  1. Create new EBS volume from the snapshot.
  2. Attach the volume to an EC2 instance as the appropriate device.
  3. Mount and verify file system integrity, then update DNS or instance mappings.
Common misconception
Snapshots alone aren't bootable until used to create a volume; AMIs package boot capability.

screens.title: RDS Automated Backups and Point-in-Time Recovery
screens.subtitle: How RDS stores daily snapshots and transaction logs for recovery

narration.text: Amazon RDS provides automated backups that perform a daily full snapshot plus continuous transaction log capture so you can perform point‑in‑time recovery within the retention window. This means you can restore a database to a specific second within the retention period, which is critical for databases with low RPO requirements. Manual snapshots are also available and persist until explicitly deleted; use them for long‑term recovery points or before risky schema changes. For greater durability, configure cross‑region automated backups so your database snapshots and logs are copied to another region automatically. A concrete example: with automated backups enabled and a seven‑day retention window, you can recover to any second within the past week; if your compliance requires a year of retention, add manual snapshots or copy automated recovery points to a cross‑region vault and extend retention there. A common mistake is relying solely on automated backups without verifying restore permissions or KMS key access in the target region. Always run restores to an isolated test instance to confirm that snapshots and logs are usable. Takeaway: RDS automated backups plus transaction logs provide robust point‑in‑time recovery, but you must plan retention, cross‑region copies, and regular restore validation.

keyIdea.title: RDS PITR
keyIdea.text: Automated daily snapshots plus transaction logs enable precise point‑in‑time restores; test restores and plan cross‑region retention.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › RDS Automated Backups and PITR
Core Concept

Automated backups + transaction logs = point‑in‑time recovery

RDS retains a daily snapshot and streams transaction logs so you can restore to a precise moment within retention.

Behavior
  • Daily full snapshot captured automatically.
  • Transaction logs stored throughout the day to enable PITR.
  • Retention configurable up to 35 days for automated backups.
Example scenario
If a schema change was applied at 10:21:32 UTC and you need the state at 10:20:00 UTC, restore using PITR to that second within the retention window.
Key takeaway
Automated backups with logs let you recover to a specific second — essential for low RPOs.
Common mistake
Not verifying KMS key and cross‑region permissions before relying on cross‑region restores.
Pro tip
Use manual snapshots for long‑term snapshots you must retain beyond the automated window.

screens.title: S3 Versioning, Cross-Region Replication, and Glacier
screens.subtitle: Protecting objects: versions, replication, and archival storage

narration.text: S3 has features that address object-level protection and long-term retention. Versioning keeps a full history of object changes in the same bucket, protecting against accidental deletes or overwrites. Cross‑Region Replication asynchronously copies new objects to a destination bucket in another region, which provides geographic redundancy and supports compliance when data must live in a different jurisdiction. For archival retention and cost savings, S3 Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive offer very low-cost storage for infrequently accessed backups. Pairing versioning with CRR is a common design: enable versioning on both source and destination buckets, configure an IAM role for replication, and specify server‑side encryption at the destination using a customer‑managed KMS key to satisfy security requirements. A mistake to avoid is enabling replication without versioning — CRR requires versioning and will not protect object history otherwise. Another pitfall is forgetting lifecycle transitions: move older versions to Glacier after a defined period to control costs. Example: enable versioning on a sensitive bucket, create a replication rule to a bucket in another region and account, and add a lifecycle rule that moves older object versions to Glacier Deep Archive after 180 days. Takeaway: combine versioning, CRR, server‑side encryption, and lifecycle transitions to meet both durability and cost objectives.

keyIdea.title: S3 protection pattern
keyIdea.text: Use Versioning + CRR + lifecycle transitions to Glacier for durable, cost-effective object backup and archival.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › S3 Versioning, CRR & Glacier
Core tools

Versioning and Cross‑Region Replication

Versioning preserves object history; CRR copies objects to a geographically separate bucket for redundancy.

Requirements
Enable versioning on both source and destination; create IAM role for replication permissions; set destination encryption.
Example
Replicate customer data from us-west-2 to us-east-1 in a separate account, encrypt destination with a CMK owned by the DR account.
Lifecycle and archival
Transition older object versions to Glacier or Glacier Deep Archive to reduce storage cost while retaining compliance snapshots.
Checklist
  • Enable versioning on both buckets.
  • Create IAM role with replication permissions and attach bucket policy on destination.
  • Configure lifecycle rules to move older versions to Glacier after policy-defined days.
Common mistake
Replicating without versioning or forgetting to configure destination encryption and permissions.

screens.title: AWS Backup: Centralized Backup Plans
screens.subtitle: Using AWS Backup to manage multiple resource types and copy actions

narration.text: AWS Backup gives you a single control plane for defining backup plans, schedules, lifecycle transitions, and copy actions across many AWS resources — EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, Storage Gateway, and S3. Instead of setting policies per service, you define backup rules in one place and attach resources via backup selections. This centralization simplifies auditing and implementing cross‑region and cross‑account copy actions. For example, you can create a backup plan with a daily rule that stores recent backups for 30 days, moves older recovery points to cold storage after seven days, and includes a copy action to a backup vault ARN in a DR account and region with a longer retention policy. Cross‑account copies require appropriate IAM and resource policies on the destination vault, but once configured they provide strong isolation. A common misconception is that AWS Backup removes the need to understand service‑specific backup semantics — it does not. You still need to know that RDS offers PITR and that EBS snapshots are incremental. AWS Backup simply coordinates schedules, retention, lifecycle, and copy actions across those service-specific mechanisms. Takeaway: AWS Backup is ideal for governance and centralized lifecycle management, but pair it with service-level knowledge and restore testing.

keyIdea.title: Centralization benefit
keyIdea.text: AWS Backup coordinates schedules, retention, lifecycle, and cross-account copies while leveraging each service's native backup capabilities.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › AWS Backup: Centralized Plans
Core Concept

One plan to manage many resources

Define schedules, lifecycle, and copy actions centrally and attach resources with backup selections.

Example rule
Daily backups → keep 30 days locally → move to cold storage after 7 days → copy to DR vault in another account and region with 365 day retention.
Operational notes
  • Destination vaults require resource policies for cross‑account access.
  • Encryption keys must be available in the target account and region for copies to succeed.
  • Restore workflows still rely on service-specific restore steps (e.g., RDS PITR, EBS volume creation).
Key takeaway
Use AWS Backup for governance and consistent retention, but validate service-level behavior during restores.

screens.title: Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) for EBS
screens.subtitle: Automating EBS snapshot creation, retention, and cross-region copy

narration.text: Data Lifecycle Manager automates snapshot creation, retention, and cross‑region copy rules for EBS volumes and AMIs. A typical policy targets volumes by tag, defines a schedule, a retention rule, and optional cross‑region copy actions. For example, tag production volumes with Environment: Production and Backup: True, then create a DLM schedule to create snapshots daily at 03:00 UTC, retain local snapshots for 30 days, and copy snapshots to us-east-1 with a 90‑day retention. The cross‑region copy configuration should include encryption settings and optionally a KMS key ARN in the target region. Implementing DLM reduces human error and ensures snapshots exist on a predictable schedule. Common mistakes include forgetting to encrypt cross‑region copies or not specifying the correct target region or KMS key, which causes copies to fail silently in some workflows. It's also important to ensure that snapshot tagging and resource selection logic actually matches intended volumes; misconfigured tags lead to missed backups. Takeaway: use DLM to automate snapshot lifecycles and cross‑region copies, verify tags, and test restore paths periodically to confirm the snapshots are usable. Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) for EBS means automate consistent, tag-driven ebs snapshot schedules and cross-region copies to reduce manual errors and ensure dr readiness.. In practical terms, automating ebs snapshot creation, retention, and cross-region copy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DLM value
keyIdea.text: Automate consistent, tag-driven EBS snapshot schedules and cross-region copies to reduce manual errors and ensure DR readiness.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › DLM for EBS
Process

Tag → Schedule → Retain → Copy

Use tags to target resources, define create and retain rules, and add cross‑region copy rules with encryption settings.

Example DLM JSON
{
  "Description": "Daily snapshots for Production EBS volumes with cross-region copy",
  "State": "ENABLED",
  "TargetTags": [
    {"Key": "Environment", "Value": "Production"},
    {"Key": "Backup", "Value": "True"}
  ],
  "PolicyDetails": {
    "PolicyType": "EBS_SNAPSHOT_MANAGEMENT",
    "ResourceTypes": ["VOLUME"],
    "Schedules": [
      {
        "Name": "DailySnapshotSchedule",
        "CreateRule": {"Interval": 24, "IntervalUnit": "HOURS", "Times": ["03:00"]},
        "RetainRule": {"Count": 30},
        "CrossRegionCopyRules": [
          {"TargetRegion": "us-east-1","RetainRule": {"Count": 90},"Encrypted": true}
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
Checklist & tips
  • Use consistent tags for selection; confirm they match actual volume tags.
  • Specify target region and KMS key ARN for encrypted copies.
  • Test restores from both local and copied snapshots regularly.
Common mistake
Assuming copies are encrypted by default in the target region without specifying encryption or a target CMK.

screens.title: Backup plan JSON for cross-region RDS copies
screens.subtitle: Practical AWS Backup plan that copies RDS recovery points to a DR vault

narration.text: Let's walk through a concrete backup plan JSON used to copy RDS recovery points to a backup vault in a different account and region. The plan defines a named rule, a schedule expression for timing, windows for start and completion, and lifecycle settings for local retention and cold storage. Crucially it contains a CopyActions array with the DestinationBackupVaultArn pointing to the DR account and region. In practice you would create this plan in the primary account, then attach backup selections for the RDS resources. The destination vault ARN must exist, and the DR account must allow the source account to put recovery points into the vault. A common misconception is assuming setting the ARN is sufficient; you must set IAM roles and resource policies on the destination vault and ensure KMS keys are usable across accounts. Example usage: the plan runs daily at 05:00 UTC, retains local copies for 30 days, moves to cold storage after 7 days, and creates a cross‑region copy retained for 365 days in the DR vault. After creating the plan, schedule a restore drill to a test DB instance in the DR region to verify encryption and permissions. Takeaway: the JSON encodes schedule, lifecycle, and copy actions — but operational success depends on vault policy and KMS configuration in both accounts.

keyIdea.title: Plan must include policies
keyIdea.text: Define schedule, lifecycle, and copy actions in the plan and verify destination vault permissions and KMS availability in the DR account.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › Backup plan JSON
Example AWS Backup plan snippet
{
  "BackupPlanName": "MyRDSBackupPlan",
  "Rules": [
    {
      "RuleName": "DailyRDSBackup",
      "TargetBackupVaultName": "Default",
      "ScheduleExpression": "cron(0 5 ? * * *)",
      "StartWindowMinutes": 60,
      "CompletionWindowMinutes": 180,
      "Lifecycle": {"DeleteAfterDays": 30, "MoveToColdStorageAfterDays": 7},
      "CopyActions": [
        {
          "DestinationBackupVaultArn": "arn:aws:backup:us-east-1:123456789012:backup-vault:DRBackupVault",
          "Lifecycle": {"DeleteAfterDays": 365}
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
Important checks
  • Destination vault exists in the DR account and region.
  • Vault resource policy allows source account to copy recovery points.
  • Destination KMS key is configured and grants decrypt to restore roles.
Restore test
After copies are created, perform a restore to an isolated DB in the DR region to validate integrity and permissions.

screens.title: EBS Snapshots vs AMIs vs RDS Snapshots
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right backup primitive for the workload

narration.text: Choosing the right backup primitive depends on what you need to restore and how quickly. EBS snapshots are block-level backups of volumes; they are incremental and optimized for storage but require creating a new volume to restore. AMIs are templates that bundle a root snapshot and launch configuration — they are ideal when you need to redeploy instances with preinstalled software quickly. RDS automated backups combine daily snapshots with transaction logs to enable point‑in‑time recovery for databases, which makes them the correct choice when you need millisecond-accurate data recovery. A common misconception is thinking AMIs replace snapshots for databases — they do not. Databases require consistent, transactionally aware backups, which RDS automated backups and transaction logs provide. Example decision: for a stateless web server, maintain AMIs for rapid scaling and EBS snapshots for attached persistent caches; for a PostgreSQL database, rely on RDS automated backups with PITR and copy snapshots to a DR vault. When designing DR, map RPO and RTO to these primitives: snapshots and AMIs typically yield higher RTOs, while RDS PITR supports tighter RPOs. Takeaway: align backup type with recovery target — instance template, volume restore, or database point‑in‑time restore — and automate accordingly.

keyIdea.title: Choose by recovery target
keyIdea.text: AMIs for instance rebuilds, EBS snapshots for block restoration, RDS automated backups for database PITR.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › EBS vs AMI vs RDS
EBS Snapshots
Incremental block backups. Restore by creating a new volume. Best for file systems and volume-level recovery.
AMIs
Instance templates that include boot configuration. Use for quick redeploy of application servers and scale-out images.
RDS Snapshots
Daily snapshots + transaction logs for point‑in‑time recovery. Required for tight database RPOs.
Decision guidance
  • Map RPO/RTO to primitives: RDS PITR for low RPO, AMIs for redeploy speed, snapshots for volume recovery.
  • Automate and test each restore path; do not assume compatibility across primitives.
  • Remember cross‑region copies and encryption when durability and isolation are required.

screens.title: Cross-Account and Cross-Region Copies
screens.subtitle: Isolation, vault policies, and KMS considerations

narration.text: Cross‑account and cross‑region copies provide isolation and geographic redundancy but require careful policy and key management. Storing backups in a separate 'DR account' protects them from accidental or malicious deletion in the primary account. To implement this, create a backup vault or S3 destination in the DR account, grant the source account permissions to write recovery points via a vault resource policy or S3 bucket policy, and ensure the destination KMS key allows encryption and decryption for the required principals. An operational example: configure AWS Backup copy actions to a vault ARN in us-east-1 owned by account 123456789012, add a resource policy on the vault permitting the source backup role to PutBackupVaultLockConfiguration and PutBackupVaultNotifications, and set up a cross‑account KMS key policy allowing encrypt for the backup service. Common pitfalls include missing resource policy statements or forgetting to enable KMS key grants for cross‑account use, which causes copies to fail. Always test the full copy and restore sequence into the DR account and region to validate permissions and KMS behavior. Takeaway: cross‑account copies strengthen isolation, but success depends on vault policies and cross‑account KMS configuration — verify both before relying on copies for DR.

keyIdea.title: Isolation matters
keyIdea.text: DR vaults in separate accounts and regions protect backups, but require explicit vault policies and KMS grants to function.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › Cross-Account & Cross-Region Copies
Implementation checklist
  1. Create destination vault or bucket in DR account and region.
  2. Attach a resource policy that allows the source account's backup role to write copies.
  3. Configure a KMS key in the target account and add key policy grants for the backup role and restore principals.
  4. Confirm COPY actions reference the destination vault ARN and test a restore into the DR account.
Example risk
If the destination KMS key denies access, the copy will fail even if vault policies are correct.
Key takeaway
Cross‑account copies provide isolation but must be validated end‑to‑end including KMS and vault policies.

screens.title: Testing Restores and Common Pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Why testing matters and what failures usually reveal

narration.text: Testing restores is where backup programs succeed or fail. Backups are only valuable if you can restore them reliably and within required time windows. A test restore should include creating a new volume from an EBS snapshot and mounting it, restoring an RDS snapshot or PITR to a test instance, and restoring S3 objects from versioned or replicated buckets. Key failure modes uncovered by drills include IAM permission gaps that prevent creating volumes or restoring databases, missing KMS grants that block decryption in the target region or account, incomplete configuration steps in a runbook, and corrupted or incomplete snapshots. Regular drills also validate retention policies so you don't discover expired recovery points in an incident. Practical advice: run restores in an isolated environment that mirrors production networking and IAM; record timings to verify RTO targets; and maintain a post‑mortem log capturing issues such as missing secrets or configuration steps. A common misconception is assuming a successful snapshot creation guarantees a successful restore; snapshots must be restored and validated. Takeaway: schedule and automate restore drills, log results, and iterate on your runbooks to reduce restore time and surprises during real incidents.

keyIdea.title: Test early, test often
keyIdea.text: Run scheduled, documented restore drills to surface permission, encryption, and configuration issues before an incident.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › Testing Restores

Restore drill checklist

EBS test
Create volume from snapshot, attach, mount, and verify data integrity.
RDS test
Restore snapshot or perform PITR to test DB instance and validate application connectivity.
S3 test
Retrieve older versions or objects from replicated buckets and validate object integrity.
Common findings
Missing IAM permissions, KMS key access issues, incomplete runbook steps, and expired recovery points.
Key takeaway
A backup that is not restored periodically is an untested assumption. Validate restores end-to-end.

screens.title: Activity: Configure automated cross-region EBS snapshot backup
screens.subtitle: Write and apply a DLM policy that snapshots, retains, and copies to us-east-1

narration.text: This hands‑on activity guides you through automating daily snapshots for EBS volumes tagged Environment: Production and Backup: True, retaining them for 30 days locally, and copying them to us‑east‑1 with 90‑day retention. Start by creating a JSON policy that targets volumes by tag, includes a schedule creating snapshots at 03:00 UTC, sets a RetainRule count of 30 for the primary region, and adds a CrossRegionCopyRules entry for us‑east‑1 with Count 90 and Encrypted true. Save the JSON and use the AWS CLI create-lifecycle-policy command to apply it in us‑west‑2. Verify snapshots appear in the primary region and test that cross‑region copies land in us‑east‑1. Practical considerations: specify a target CMK ARN in the copy rule if the target requires a customer-managed key, and confirm IAM roles and permissions for cross‑region snapshot copy. After creation, perform a restore from a copied snapshot in us‑east‑1 to validate the copied snapshot is usable and the encryption key is accessible. Common error: forgetting to grant the target CMK decrypt permissions to the restore principal. Takeaway: automation with DLM reduces toil, but ensure permissions and KMS configuration are validated with a restore test.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Create a DLM policy that snapshots production volumes daily, retains locally, and copies encrypted snapshots to us-east-1 for extended retention.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › Activity: DLM policy

Task: Create and apply a DLM policy

Follow these steps to automate daily snapshots and cross‑region copies.

1. Author policy JSON
Save a JSON file similar to the earlier example that defines TargetTags, CreateRule, RetainRule, and CrossRegionCopyRules.
2. Apply with CLI
aws dlm create-lifecycle-policy --region us-west-2 --cli-input-json file://dlm-policy.json
3. Verify and test
Confirm snapshots are created, confirm copies appear in us-east-1, and restore a copied snapshot to validate KMS and data integrity.
Key takeaway
Automate snapshot lifecycles, then validate by performing restores in the target region and account.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from Backup and Restore Strategies

narration.text: These three key concepts summarize the chapter. First, EBS snapshots and AMIs serve different roles: snapshots for block-level recovery and AMIs for instance templates used in rapid rebuilds. Second, RDS automated backups plus transaction logs enable point‑in‑time recovery, which is essential for low RPOs; manual snapshots extend retention beyond automated windows. Third, centralized tools like AWS Backup and automation via DLM let you schedule, retain, and copy backups across regions and accounts, but success requires explicit vault policies, KMS configuration, and restore testing. Keep these ideas in mind when designing your backup program: match primitives to recovery targets, automate lifecycle and cross‑account copies for isolation, and run restores to validate everything. These principles will help you build a backup strategy that is practical, auditable, and resilient. narration.text: Before you finish the chapter, keep three operational reminders in mind. First, automate backups by tagging and using DLM or AWS Backup so human error doesn't create gaps. Second, enforce isolation by copying critical recovery points to a separate account and region with proper vault policies and KMS grants. Third, schedule and document restore drills that validate every recovery path — snapshots, AMIs, RDS PITR, and S3 object restores — and log what failed and why. These practices convert backups from a checkbox into a reliable recovery capability. Ask yourself: can your team restore a critical service within the required RTO using the available recovery points? If not, iterate on automation, retention, and testing until the answer is yes.
